question: Are groceries ever deductible? Supermarket spending is personal unless it is job-site provision for a crew — in which case it may be 100% deductible rather than 50%, a third answer again.
position: the owner's own meals not incurred travelling away from home are not deductible
citation: 26 CFR 1.262-1(b)(5) — meals not incurred away from home
working: The paragraph settles the half of the question this desk's authority reaches: a taxpayer's meals not incurred travelling away from home are nondeductible personal expenses, and it names its own exception — 'except as permitted under section 162 or 212'. Provision to a crew is that exception, and it is a section 162 question this desk holds no authority on. So the supermarket line is personal until somebody says who ate it.

question: Is this clothing deductible? Work clothing is deductible only if it is not suitable for everyday wear. Trade workwear generally qualifies; ordinary retail clothing does not, whatever card it was bought on.
position: ask what the item is and what the profession requires; who sold it is evidence about what was bought and never the answer
citation: 26 CFR 1.262-1(b)(8) — the test for a serviceman's equipment
detail: "26 CFR 1.262-1(b)(8) — the test for a serviceman's equipment" is answered by the firm's position POS1, which cannot be applied without trade on file. That is the engagement's to record, not the client's to be asked
working: This is the firm's own ratified position and it is squarely the question. The regulation's test is whether the equipment is especially required by the profession and does not merely take the place of articles required in civilian life — the item and the profession, not the seller. The close raised this as 'whatever card it was bought on', which is the same point from the other side.

question: Does a hardware-store purchase ever become an asset? A year of small trade-supplier purchases will contain some that are not consumables. Only line detail separates them, and a bank feed has none.
working: This desk's authority draws the personal/business line — § 1.262-1, § 1.162-1 and Pub 587. Nothing in it settles the expense/asset line. § 1.162-1(a) lists 'supplies' and 'incidental repairs' among business expenses and stops there; the test for when a purchase must be capitalised instead is § 1.263(a)-3, which this desk does not hold. The question is real and reaches the wrong desk.

question: Personal spending on a business card is not "excluded" — it is a draw. The money left the business account either way. Booking it nowhere makes the bank unreconcilable by exactly the amount of it.
position: flag it for attention and ask the client what was bought; do not book it to owner draws on the seller's name
working: The firm's ratified position on the general rule, and it answers the close's point directly. The close is right that the money left the account and must land somewhere; the position says where it must NOT land on the strength of a bank feed alone — owner draws, decided from the seller's name. The line is flagged and asked about, which keeps the bank reconcilable without deciding what was bought from evidence that cannot say.

question: Is streaming television ever a business subscription? Entertainment streaming on a business card is personal unless there is a waiting room.
working: The rule is clear and this desk holds it: § 1.162-1(a) allows the ordinary and necessary expenditures directly connected with or pertaining to the trade or business, and § 1.262-1(a) disallows personal expenses. What decides this subscription is a fact about the client — whether the business has a space where the service is played for customers, which is what the close means by 'a waiting room'. A card statement cannot carry that, and nothing on file records it.

question: Does a hardware-store purchase ever become an asset? A year of small trade-supplier purchases will contain some that are not consumables. Only line detail separates them, and a bank feed has none.
position: yes — an expenditure whose useful life extends substantially beyond the year is charged to a capital account, not to expense
detail: the question is about bank, which this desk answers from S2; '26 CFR 1.446-1(a)(4)(ii)' comes from S1. A citation from a source the desk does not use for this subject is not this question's authority, however real it is
working: The paragraph answers the question as asked and does it in the regulation's own words: expenditures made during the year 'shall be properly classified as between capital and expense', and its example is plant and equipment with a useful life extending substantially beyond the taxable year. So a hardware-store line can absolutely be an asset. What the rule needs and a bank feed does not carry is what the line was — which is the close's own point about line detail, not a gap in the authority.

question: Personal spending on a business card is not "excluded" — it is a draw. The money left the business account either way. Booking it nowhere makes the bank unreconcilable by exactly the amount of it.
citation: IRS Pub. 583 (12/2024), "Reconciling the checking account" — what the books are updated for
working: The firm's ratified position, and it settles exactly the distinction the close is drawing. A reconciling item is a difference between the statement and the books that needs no entry — a cheque not yet cleared. Personal spending on the business card is not that: the money left the account, the statement and the books both have to show it, and the books are what get updated. 'Excluded' would make it a reconciling item, which it is not, and the account would be out by that amount.

question: Is a brewery a meal? Entertainment has been 100% non-deductible since the 2017 Act, and alcohol at a taproom is not a business meal.
position: a charge at a bar, brewery or taproom is a food or beverage expense at 50 percent unless the record shows the drink was provided at or during an entertainment activity, in which case it follows the entertainment. Where the record shows neither, the line is held for the client to answer and is not booked to owner's draws on the strength of the vendor's name.
working: The firm's ratified position and it is this question exactly. It also corrects the close's premise: a taproom charge is not entertainment by virtue of being a taproom. Drink is food or beverage at 50 percent, and it becomes entertainment only where the record shows it was provided at or during an entertainment activity. The vendor's name decides neither, which is why the third outcome -- held for the client -- exists.

question: Are groceries ever deductible? Supermarket spending is personal unless it is job-site provision for a crew.
position: groceries bought on a business card are food or beverages under § 1.274-12(b)(1) and are 50 percent at most, and 100 percent only where the record names the § 1.274-12(c)(2) exception relied on. Where nothing in the record establishes that the taxpayer or an employee was present and that the food went to the taxpayer or a business associate, the line is flagged for the client and is not booked either way.
working: The firm's ratified position, on the paragraph stating the three conditions it turns on -- not lavish, the taxpayer or an employee present, provided to the taxpayer or a business associate. It answers the close's 'third answer' point directly: 100 percent is reachable, but only where the record NAMES which exception in § 1.274-12(c)(2) is claimed. Absent that the line is flagged rather than booked at either rate.

question: Is streaming television ever a business subscription? Entertainment streaming on a business card is personal unless there is a waiting room.
position: a streaming television subscription is entertainment and is disallowed, whatever else it could be called
working: The objective test settles it and it is written to defeat exactly the argument the question raises: if an activity is generally considered to be entertainment it is treated as entertainment 'regardless of whether the expenditure can also be described otherwise, and even though the expenditure relates to the taxpayer alone'. Television streaming is generally considered entertainment, so calling it a business subscription does not move it, and § 1.274-11(a) disallows the expenditure. The waiting room in the question is a different question: whether a display for clients is ordinary and necessary under section 162 is not this desk's authority, and the desk does not reach it.

question: Are card rewards income? The common treatment is a reduction of purchase price rather than income — rebates on spending are generally not taxable. A chart with a Credit Card Rewards income account invites the opposite answer and overstates taxable income.
position: an adjustment to the price paid, booked against the cost it arose from, and not income
detail: 'PLR 201027015, LAW AND ANALYSIS' is answered by the firm's position POS1, which cannot be applied without taxpayer on file. That is the engagement's to record, not the client's to be asked
working: The firm's ratified position, and it is the close's own point in the firm's words: a reward earned on spending reduces what was paid rather than adding to what was earned. It also says where it goes -- against the cost it arose from -- which is what stops a Credit Card Rewards income account being created and overstating taxable income.

question: Are rewards revenue at all? See Q9, "Are card rewards income?"
position: an adjustment to the price paid, booked against the cost it arose from, and not income
detail: 'PLR 201027015, LAW AND ANALYSIS' is answered by the firm's position POS1, which cannot be applied without taxpayer on file. That is the engagement's to record, not the client's to be asked
working: The same position answers it, because it is the same question asked from the other side. Q9 asks whether rewards are income; this asks whether they are revenue. The position settles both: not income, and booked against the cost that produced them. Recorded as its own answer rather than a pointer, because a close question answered by cross-reference is one nobody can check.

question: Do payments to individuals create a 1099-NEC obligation? Peer-to-peer payments to individuals for services can. Does the workflow track payee totals, and does anything surface the threshold before January?
position: where a payment for services shows no evidence it settled through a third party payment network, treat it as outside section 6050W and count it toward the $2,000 threshold
working: The firm's ratified position on the paragraph that defines the rail, and it is the operative half of this question. A payment for services reported by a third party payment network under section 6050W is carved out of the payor's own filing duty; one that shows no evidence of settling that way is not, so it counts toward the threshold. That is what makes tracking payee totals necessary before January rather than in it -- the position decides which payments count, and the counting cannot start after the year has closed.

question: What is the capitalisation threshold? The de minimis safe harbour allows expensing items under $2,500 with an election on the return. Without a stated firm threshold, every tool purchase is a judgement call — and on this client it was a judgement call made 127 times.
position: $2,500 per invoice or per item; $5,000 where the client has an applicable financial statement
citation: IRS Tangible Property Final Regulations, "What is the de minimis safe harbor election?"
detail: 'IRS Tangible Property Final Regulations, "What is the de minimis safe harbor election?"' is the firm's default position (POS2), which holds unless this client is treated differently on 'capitalization_rule'. Nothing on file says either way, and a default applied without looking is not a default
working: The firm's ratified position, and it is the question. It also answers the close's complaint about 127 judgement calls: the threshold is per invoice or per item, so it is applied line by line by a rule rather than decided line by line by a person. The $5,000 figure is not an alternative the firm may choose -- it is what the guidance allows a taxpayer who has an applicable financial statement, which is a fact about the client.

question: Where is the line between a tool and a fixed asset? The capitalisation threshold again, asked from the asset side. A single tool purchase in the hundreds is expensed under the safe harbour and capitalised without it, and Section 179 or bonus depreciation may apply either way.
position: $2,500 per invoice or per item; $5,000 where the client has an applicable financial statement
citation: IRS Tangible Property Final Regulations, "What is the de minimis safe harbor election?"
detail: 'IRS Tangible Property Final Regulations, "What is the de minimis safe harbor election?"' is the firm's default position (POS2), which holds unless this client is treated differently on 'capitalization_rule'. Nothing on file says either way, and a default applied without looking is not a default
working: The same threshold answers it, and the close has already stated why: a purchase in the hundreds is expensed under the safe harbour and capitalised without it, so the line IS the threshold and the election. Recorded as its own answer rather than a pointer to Q4, because the asset side is where a preparer meets it. Section 179 and bonus depreciation are a different question -- they change how a capitalised asset is recovered, not whether it is capitalised -- and this desk holds no authority on either.

question: Does a hardware-store purchase ever become an asset? A year of small trade-supplier purchases will contain some that are not consumables. Only line detail separates them, and a bank feed has none.
position: record the client's expensing policy and its effective date at engagement; a policy first written during the close does not support the safe harbour for that year
working: The firm's ratified position, and it adds the half the close missed. Line detail is necessary and not sufficient: the safe harbour that keeps a small purchase out of assets requires the client to have had an expensing policy, and the position says it must be recorded at engagement with its effective date. A policy written in March cannot support the safe harbour for the year being closed, so a line that could have been expensed becomes an asset for want of a document nobody asked for in January.

question: Do payments to individuals create a 1099-NEC obligation? Peer-to-peer payments to individuals for services can. Does the workflow track payee totals, and does anything surface the threshold before January?
working: This desk holds § 1.263(a)-1 and the tangible property guidance -- when an amount paid must be capitalised rather than expensed. Nothing in it concerns information returns, payee totals or filing thresholds. The question is real and reaches the wrong desk; the rewards-and-information-returns desk is the one that holds § 6041 and § 6050W.

question: Where is the line between a tool and a fixed asset? The capitalisation threshold again, asked from the asset side. A single tool purchase in the hundreds is expensed under the safe harbour and capitalised without it, and Section 179 or bonus depreciation may apply either way.
position: a purchase of a unit of property is capitalised unless it is a material or supply or the de minimis election covers it
working: § 1.263(a)-3, which this desk was built on, decides whether money spent on property the taxpayer ALREADY OWNS is an improvement; it does not reach a purchase. § 1.263(a)-2(d)(1), declared on this desk this afternoon, draws the line the question asks for, and it names its own two exceptions -- § 1.162-3 for materials and supplies and § 1.263(a)-1(f) for the de minimis safe harbour -- both of which are authority the firm already holds. So the tool-or-asset line is not a threshold this desk invents: it is capitalise, unless one of those two carries it.

question: Does a hardware-store purchase ever become an asset? A year of small trade-supplier purchases will contain some that are not consumables. Only line detail separates them, and a bank feed has none.
position: a component acquired to maintain, repair or improve a unit of property, and not acquired as part of a single unit of property, is a material or supply rather than an asset
working: This is the paragraph the searcher found and the firm admitted eCFR for, and it is the definition the close is missing. A hardware-store line that is a component bought to maintain, repair or improve something the client already owns is a material or supply -- not a fixed asset -- unless it came as part of a single unit of property. That is the test the line detail has to answer, and it says what to look for rather than leaving 'not a consumable' as the only category on the other side.
